key_points.text: Waterfall: stages are done in order and each is signed off before the next. Clear structure, documentation and deadlines; suits projects with fixed, well-understood requirements. Drawbacks: the user sees little until the end and changes are expensive to make once a stage is finished.

Agile methodologies build the software in short iterations with regular feedback from the client, so changing requirements can be handled. Suits projects where requirements are unclear or likely to change; drawbacks are less documentation and the need for the client to be closely involved.

Extreme programming (an agile method) uses short iterations, pair programming, writing tests before code, and a customer representative in the team. It produces high-quality code but needs a committed client and is costly in programmer time.

Spiral model: each loop plans, analyses risks, builds and evaluates a bigger version. Good for large, high-risk projects because risks are tackled early; drawbacks are the cost of risk analysis and the expertise it needs.

Rapid application development builds prototypes quickly and refines them with user feedback until one becomes the final system. Good when users are available and the interface matters; less suited to large or safety-critical systems, and the code can be less efficient.

Algorithms can be written as pseudocode, a flowchart or program code. In the exam, code is shown in OCR's pseudocode style, but your answers don't need to be syntactically perfect as long as they use appropriate structures.

dont_confuse.text: Waterfall vs agile: waterfall finishes each stage once, in order; agile repeats short cycles and expects requirements to change.
RAD vs spiral: RAD is driven by user feedback on prototypes; spiral is driven by risk analysis on each loop.
Agile vs extreme programming: agile is the family of approaches; extreme programming is one specific agile method.
